source: Dionysii Cartusiani Opera Omnia, t. VI (Montreuil)

44.title: EXPOSITIO PSALMI QUADRAGESIMI QUARTI : ERUCTAVIT COR MEUM.
44.title_en: Exposition of the forty-fourth psalm: My heart hath uttered.

paras.t: Psalmus jam elucidandus, tali titulo prænotatur : In finem, pro his qui commutabuntur filiis Core, ad intellectum, canticum pro dilecto. Psalmus iste gloriosus ac nobilis, de duplici Christi natura, ac divina generatione ipsius, et de unitate personæ ipsius, de conjunctione quoque Christi sponsi et sponsæ suæ Ecclesiæ, seu Virginis gloriosæ, aut fidelis animæ, excellenter evidenterque tractat : et ideo appellatur epithalamium, id est carmen thalami, nuptias Sponsi ac Sponsæ collaudans.
paras.en: The psalm now to be explained is headed with this title: [[44:1|Unto the end|In finem]], [[44:1|for them that shall be changed|pro his qui commutabuntur]], [[44:1|for the sons of Core|filiis Core]], [[44:1|for understanding|ad intellectum]], [[44:1|A canticle for the Beloved|canticum pro dilecto]]. This glorious and noble psalm treats excellently and plainly of the two natures of Christ and of his divine generation, and of the unity of his person, and also of the union of Christ the bridegroom with his bride, the Church, or the glorious Virgin, or the faithful soul: and therefore it is called an epithalamium, that is, a bridal song [*carmen thalami*, literally "song of the bridal chamber"], praising the marriage of the Bridegroom and the Bride.

paras.t: Sensus ergo tituli talis est : Canticum, in finem, id est psalmus iste, qui dicitur canticum, tendens in Christum, qui est principium nostræ creationis, et finis nostræ recreationis : canticum, inquam, scriptum pro his qui commutabuntur, id est pro electis, qui non solum resurgent, sed etiam immutabuntur, id est, beatam immortalitatem adipiscentur, videlicet pro filiis Core, id est imitatoribus Christi in loco Calvariæ crucifixi. Core enim interpretatur Calvaria. Pro dilecto : id est, canticum istud etiam scriptum est pro Christo, ad quem Pater dixit : Tu es Filius meus carissimus. Sic ergo canticum istud est pro Christo et fidelibus ejus, id est, de Sponso Ecclesiæ et ipsa Ecclesia loquitur. Ad intellectum, id est, quatenus Christi fideles sapienter intelligant Christum, et ejus mysteria, scilicet incarnationem, et conjunctionem cum Ecclesia, fideliter contemplentur. Hieronymus autem in translatione sua juxta Hebræum, ponit hunc titulum : Victori, pro liliis filiorum Core, eruditionis canticum amantissimum : et redit in idem cum titulo præinducto. Per lilia enim intelliguntur fidelia Christi membra, quæ sunt filii Sponsæ.
paras.en: The sense of the title, then, is this: [[44:1|A canticle|Canticum]], [[44:1|unto the end|in finem]], that is, this psalm, which is called a canticle, tending towards Christ, who is the beginning of our creation and the end of our re-creation: a canticle, I say, written [[44:1|for them that shall be changed|pro his qui commutabuntur]], that is, for the elect, who will not only rise again but will also be changed, that is, will attain blessed immortality; namely [[44:1|for the sons of Core|pro filiis Core]], that is, for the imitators of Christ crucified in the place of Calvary. For *Core* is interpreted *Calvary* [the name was taken to mean "baldness", whence Calvary, the bare "place of the skull"]. [[44:1|for the Beloved|Pro dilecto]]: that is, this canticle was also written for Christ, to whom the Father said: [[Luke 3:22|Thou art my beloved Son|Tu es Filius meus carissimus]][[Matt 3:17||]][[Matt 17:5||]][[Luke 9:35||]] [the margin gives Matt. iii, 17; xxii, 5; Luke ii, 22; ii, 35, evidently for Matt 3:17 and 17:5, Luke 3:22 and 9:35; Denis has *carissimus*, "dearest", for *dilectus*, "beloved"]. So this canticle is for Christ and for his faithful, that is, it speaks of the Bridegroom of the Church and of the Church herself. [[44:1|for understanding|Ad intellectum]], that is, so that the faithful of Christ may wisely understand Christ, and faithfully contemplate his mysteries, namely his incarnation and his union with the Church. Jerome, however, in his translation from the Hebrew, gives this title: To the victor, for the lilies of the sons of Core, a most loving canticle of instruction; and it comes to the same as the title given above. For by the lilies are understood the faithful members of Christ, who are the sons of the Bride.

paras.t: Porro exordium psalmi hujus, videlicet primi duo versus, dupliciter exponuntur. Primo, ut sint verba Dei Patris, in cujus persona loquens Propheta, ait : Eructavit cor meum verbum bonum : id est, mens mea paterna, seu ego ipse qui aliud nihil sum nisi mens paterna simplicissima atque purissima, vel intellectus meus æternus, sive memoria mea fecunda, de plenitudine suæ infinitæ fecunditatis ac bonitatis, et de ipso fonte meæ essentiæ infinitis divitiis pleno, intellectualiter protuli, æternaliter dixi, vereque genui unicum Filium mihi consubstantialem, qui est Verbum bonum. De quo scriptum est : Fons sapientiæ Verbum Dei in excelsis ; et, In principio erat Verbum, et Verbum erat apud Deum, et Deus erat Verbum. De quo superius dictum est : Verbo Domini cœli firmati sunt. Sapiens quoque : Dum quietum silentium tenerent omnia, et nox in suo cursu medium iter haberet, omnipotens sermo tuus, Domine, de cœlo exsiliens, a regalibus sedibus venit. Dico ego, Pater æternus, opera mea, id est quæcumque ago, regi, id est Christo Filio meo amantissimo, qui est Rex regum et Dominus dominantium. Hoc est quod Christus ait : Pater diligit Filium, et omnia demonstrat ei quæ ipse facit. Quidquid enim Pater in se ipso cognoscit, hoc in Verbo suo exprimit, ita ut quidquid in Patris essentia continetur, hoc plane resplendet in Filio. Ipse namque Unigenitus, est mentis paternæ Verbum æternum, intelligentiæ dictio, et sapientiæ ejus plena expressio. Denique quidquid Pater in ordine rerum a principio condidit, hoc æternaliter in Verbo suo dixit, atque per ipsum congruo tempore fecit. Propter quod Joannes testatur : Omnia per ipsum facta sunt ; et iterum, Quod factum est, in ipso vita erat.
paras.en: Now the opening of this psalm, namely its first two verses [in this edition's count; both fall within v. 2 as numbered here], is expounded in two ways. First, so that they are the words of God the Father, in whose person the Prophet speaks and says: [[44:2|My heart hath uttered a good word|Eructavit cor meum verbum bonum]] [*eructavit*, literally "hath belched forth", that is, has poured out from its fullness]: that is, my fatherly mind, or I myself, who am nothing else but the most simple and most pure fatherly mind, or my eternal intellect, or my fruitful memory, out of the fullness of its infinite fruitfulness and goodness, and from the very fountain of my essence, full of infinite riches, have brought forth intellectually, have spoken eternally, and have truly begotten an only Son consubstantial with me, who is the good Word. Of whom it is written: [[Ecclus 1:5|The word of God on high is the fountain of wisdom|Fons sapientiæ Verbum Dei in excelsis]]; and, [[John 1:1|In the beginning was the Word: and the Word was with God: and the Word was God.|In principio erat Verbum, et Verbum erat apud Deum, et Deus erat Verbum]] Of whom it was said above: [[Ps 32:6|By the word of the Lord the heavens were established|Verbo Domini cœli firmati sunt]]. And the Wise Man too: [[Wis 18:14|while all things were in quiet silence, and the night was in the midst of her course|Dum quietum silentium tenerent omnia, et nox in suo cursu medium iter haberet]], [[Wis 18:15|thy Almighty word|omnipotens sermo tuus]], O Lord, [[Wis 18:15|leaped down from heaven from thy royal throne|de cœlo exsiliens, a regalibus sedibus venit]]. [[44:2|I speak|Dico ego]], the eternal Father, [[44:2|my works|opera mea]], that is, whatever I do, [[44:2|to the king|regi]], that is, to Christ, my most beloved Son, who is [[Apoc 19:16|King of kings and Lord of lords|Rex regum et Dominus dominantium]]. This is what Christ says: [[John 5:20|the Father loveth the Son and sheweth him all things which himself doth|Pater diligit Filium, et omnia demonstrat ei quæ ipse facit]]. For whatever the Father knows in himself, he expresses in his Word, so that whatever is contained in the Father's essence shines forth plainly in the Son. For the Only-begotten is the eternal Word of the fatherly mind, the utterance of his understanding, and the full expression of his wisdom. Lastly, whatever the Father created in the order of things from the beginning, he spoke eternally in his Word, and made through him at the fitting time. Wherefore John testifies: [[John 1:3|All things were made by him|Omnia per ipsum facta sunt]]; and again, [[John 1:3|that was made|Quod factum est]], [[John 1:4|In him was life|in ipso vita erat]] [Denis follows the old reading "What was made, in him was life", joining the last words of v. 3 to v. 4].

paras.t: Deinde ait Pater æternus : Lingua mea calamus scribæ velociter scribentis : id est, intellectus meus similis est stilo hominis cito scribentis. Et hoc propter duo. Primo, quoniam sicut verbum quod stilo scribitur, non est sonans ac transiens, sed silens, firmum ac permanens ; sic Verbum Dei Patris non est transiens, sonans atque instabile, sed secretum, firmum, immobile et æternum. Secundo, quoniam sicut stilus velociter scribentis, sine labore ac mora notabili verbum exarat ; sic intellectus divinus ad intra loquens, vel Deus Pater, sine motu, labore et mora Verbum suum produxit in ipso æternitatis momento, quemadmodum Sapientia æterna, quæ est Verbum ac Filius Dei, ait : Dominus possedit me in initio viarum suarum, antequam quidquam faceret a principio ; ab æterno ordinata sum. Nondum erant abyssi, et ego jam concepta eram.
paras.en: Then the eternal Father says: [[44:2|My tongue is the pen of a scrivener that writeth swiftly|Lingua mea calamus scribæ velociter scribentis]]: that is, my intellect is like the pen of a man who writes quickly. And this for two reasons. First, because as a word that is written with a pen is not sounding and passing, but silent, firm and lasting, so the Word of God the Father is not passing, sounding and unstable, but hidden, firm, unmoved and eternal. Second, because as the pen of one who writes swiftly traces a word without labour or noticeable delay, so the divine intellect speaking within [*ad intra*, that is, within the Godhead itself], or God the Father, brought forth his Word without movement, labour or delay, in the very instant of eternity; as eternal Wisdom, who is the Word and Son of God, says: [[Prov 8:22|The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his ways, before he made any thing from the beginning|Dominus possedit me in initio viarum suarum, antequam quidquam faceret a principio]]; [[Prov 8:23|I was set up from eternity|ab æterno ordinata sum]]. [[Prov 8:24|The depths were not as yet, and I was already conceived|Nondum erant abyssi, et ego jam concepta eram]].

paras.t: Secundo exponi potest hic locus, ut sint verba Prophetæ ; eritque sensus : Eructavit cor meum verbum bonum : id est, ex plenitudine divinæ illuminationis, et ex abundantia prophetalis notitiæ, intellectus meus protulit, intra se dixit et ore expressit psalmum præsentem, qui est verbum bonum et salubre, ac optimus sermo. Dico ego opera mea regi : id est, scripturam istam et alia cuncta quæ ago, dico, canto, et scribo ad gloriam regis Messiæ, de cujus nuptiis in hoc psalmo tractabo. Lingua mea calamus scribæ velociter scribentis : id est, lingua oris mei in scribendo hunc psalmum fuit calamus, stilus, penna, seu graphium scriptoris cito scribentis, id est mei ipsius, qui psalmum istum sine proprio studio scripsi et sine labore, secundum quod Spiritus Sanctus me docuit. Lingua enim Prophetæ fuit instrumentum animæ suæ, quemadmodum penna instrumentum est manus scribentis. Scripsitque Propheta hunc psalmum velociter, sicut apud Jeremiam habetur : Dixit Baruch ad principes Juda : Ex ore suo loquebatur Jeremias, quasi legens omnes sermones istos ad me, et ego scribebam in volumine atramento. Vel sic : Lingua mea calamus fuit scribæ velociter scribentis, id est Spiritus Sancti, qui quos ad scribendum inspirat, velociter scribere facit. Nescit enim tarda molimina Spiritus Sancti gratia, teste Ambrosio. Et huic sensui consonat quod David alio loco fatetur : Spiritus Domini locutus est per me, et sermo ejus per linguam meam.
paras.en: Second, this passage can be expounded so that they are the words of the Prophet; and the sense will be: [[44:2|My heart hath uttered a good word|Eructavit cor meum verbum bonum]]: that is, out of the fullness of divine enlightenment and the abundance of prophetic knowledge, my intellect has brought forth, has spoken within itself and expressed with the mouth, the present psalm, which is a good and wholesome word, and an excellent discourse. [[44:2|I speak my works to the king|Dico ego opera mea regi]]: that is, this writing and all the other things that I do, I speak, sing and write to the glory of the king Messias, of whose marriage I shall treat in this psalm. [[44:2|My tongue is the pen of a scrivener that writeth swiftly|Lingua mea calamus scribæ velociter scribentis]]: that is, the tongue of my mouth, in writing this psalm, was the reed, the stylus, the pen or the graver of a writer who writes quickly, that is, of myself, who wrote this psalm without study of my own and without labour, as the Holy Ghost taught me. For the Prophet's tongue was the instrument of his soul, as the pen is the instrument of the hand that writes. And the Prophet wrote this psalm swiftly, as is found in Jeremias: [[Jer 36:18|Baruch said|Dixit Baruch]] to the princes of Juda: [[Jer 36:18|With his mouth he pronounced all these words as if he were reading to me: and I wrote in a volume with ink|Ex ore suo loquebatur Jeremias, quasi legens omnes sermones istos ad me, et ego scribebam in volumine atramento]]. Or thus: [[44:2|My tongue is the pen of a scrivener that writeth swiftly|Lingua mea calamus fuit scribæ velociter scribentis]], that is, of the Holy Ghost, who makes those whom he inspires to write, write swiftly. For the grace of the Holy Ghost knows no slow labours, as Ambrose witnesses. And with this sense agrees what David confesses in another place: [[2 Kings 23:2|The spirit of the Lord hath spoken by me and his word by my tongue.|Spiritus Domini locutus est per me, et sermo ejus per linguam meam]]

paras.t: Prima autem expositio horum versuum, melior est atque profundior, et ei concordat quod per Isaiam ait Deus Pater, Egredietur de ore meo justitiæ verbum, et non revertetur ; illud quoque Ecclesiastici, Ego ex ore Altissimi prodivi primogenita ante omnem creaturam. Non solum autem dixit, Eructavit cor meum verbum ; sed, Verbum bonum : ad insinuandum quod Verbum istud sit verus Deus. Nam Christo testante : Nemo bonus nisi Deus. Ipse enim Deus est naturaliter atque quomodolibet bonus ; et secundum Dionysium, natura ejus est bonitas ; primumque Dei nomen est, bonum.
paras.en: But the first exposition of these verses is the better and the deeper, and with it agrees what God the Father says through Isaias: [[Is 45:23|the word of justice shall go out of my mouth, and shall not return|Egredietur de ore meo justitiæ verbum, et non revertetur]]; and that word of Ecclesiasticus too: [[Ecclus 24:5|I came out of the mouth of the most High, the firstborn before all creatures|Ego ex ore Altissimi prodivi primogenita ante omnem creaturam]]. And he did not say only, [[44:2|My heart hath uttered|Eructavit cor meum]] a word, but [[44:2|a good word|Verbum bonum]]: to suggest that this Word is true God. For Christ testifies: [[Mark 10:18|None is good but one, that is God|Nemo bonus nisi Deus]]. For he is God, good by nature and in every way; and according to Dionysius his nature is goodness, and the first name of God is Good.

paras.t: Consequenter prorumpit Propheta in laudem regis istius, et primo commendat eum propter pulchritudinem, dicens : Speciosus forma præ filiis hominum. Triplex speciositas in Christo fuit. Una æterna, divina et infinita : quæ convenit ei ratione divinæ naturæ, estque essentialiter idem cum divina essentia, atque in tribus Personis una ac indivisa. Et de hac pulchritudine Christi, qui est sapientia Patris, scriptum est : Sapientia emanatio quædam est omnipotentis Dei sincera. Candor est enim lucis æternæ, et speculum sine macula Dei majestatis, et imago bonitatis illius. Et Apostolus : Qui quum sit splendor gloriæ et figura substantiæ ejus, sedet ad dexteram majestatis in excelsis. Unde sanctus Hilarius appropriata divinarum personarum designans : Æternitas, inquit, est in Patre, species in imagine, usus in munere. Quid autem est, Species in imagine, nisi, Pulchritudo convenit Filio tanquam per omnia simili Deo Patri? Propter quod Filius contestatur : Qui videt me, videt et Patrem. Hoc enim ait, non propter identitatem personæ, ut asserebat inimicus sanctæ Trinitatis Sabellius, sed propter omnimodam similitudinem utriusque, secundum quod ait Apostolus : Qui est imago Dei invisibilis, primogenitus omnis creaturæ. De hac increata pulchritudine Dei Dionysius pulcherrime loquitur. Propter hanc quoque speciositatem ait de Christo Petrus apostolus : In quem desiderant angeli prospicere.
paras.en: Next the Prophet breaks out into the praise of this king, and first he commends him for his beauty, saying: [[44:3|Thou art beautiful above the sons of men|Speciosus forma præ filiis hominum]] [literally "beautiful in form"; Denis's word for this beauty is *speciositas*]. There was a threefold beauty in Christ. One is eternal, divine and infinite: it belongs to him by reason of the divine nature, and is essentially the same as the divine essence, and is one and undivided in the three Persons. And of this beauty of Christ, who is the wisdom of the Father, it is written: Wisdom is [[Wis 7:25|a certain pure emmanation of the glory of the Almighty God|emanatio quædam est omnipotentis Dei sincera]]. [[Wis 7:26|For she is the brightness of eternal light, and the unspotted mirror of God's majesty, and the image of his goodness.|Candor est enim lucis æternæ, et speculum sine macula Dei majestatis, et imago bonitatis illius]] And the Apostle: [[Heb 1:3|Who being the brightness of his glory and the figure of his substance|Qui quum sit splendor gloriæ et figura substantiæ ejus]], [[Heb 1:3|sitteth on the right hand of the majesty on high|sedet ad dexteram majestatis in excelsis]]. Hence Saint Hilary, setting out the appropriations of the divine Persons [that is, attributes common to all three but ascribed to one of them for a likeness to what is proper to him], says: Eternity is in the Father, beauty [*species*] in the Image, use [*usus*, that is, enjoyment] in the Gift. And what does "beauty in the Image" mean, if not that beauty belongs to the Son as being in all things like God the Father? Wherefore the Son testifies: [[John 14:9|he that seeth me seeth the Father also|Qui videt me, videt et Patrem]]. He says this not because of identity of person, as Sabellius, the enemy of the Holy Trinity, asserted, but because of the complete likeness of each to the other, according to what the Apostle says: [[Col 1:15|Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature|Qui est imago Dei invisibilis, primogenitus omnis creaturæ]]. Of this uncreated beauty of God Dionysius speaks most beautifully. Because of this beauty also the apostle Peter says of Christ: [[1 Pet 1:12|on whom the angels desire to look|In quem desiderant angeli prospicere]].

paras.t: Alia est speciositas Christi creata et spiritualis, quæ consistit in perfectione suæ sapientiæ, in excellentia gratiæ, et in eminentia suæ caritatis atque virtutum. Et ista speciositas Christi, summa et incomparabilis fuit, imo et major quam omnium simul electorum : quia scriptum est, Non ad mensuram dat Deus spiritum, subintelligendum est, Christo homini.
paras.en: Another beauty of Christ is created and spiritual, which consists in the perfection of his wisdom, the excellence of his grace, and the eminence of his charity and virtues. And this beauty of Christ was supreme and beyond compare, indeed greater than that of all the elect together: for it is written, [[John 3:34|God doth not give the Spirit by measure|Non ad mensuram dat Deus spiritum]]; and we must understand: to Christ as man.

paras.t: Tertia autem speciositas Christi, fuit creata et corporalis, quæ consistit in debita proportione, situ et quantitate membrorum, et in congrua superfusione vivacis coloris. Et ista pulchritudo Christi magna ac vehemens fuit. Primo, quoniam nulla naturalis perfectio defuit ei. Secundo, quia decebat ut anima illa sanctissima atque pulcherrima proportionatum sibi corpus, utpote pulchrum ac nitidum, sortiretur. Tertio, quoniam corpus Christi sumptum erat ex purissima materia, scilicet ex mundissimis sanguinibus dignissimæ Virginis. Quarto, quia formatum compactumque fuit ab agente infallibili, non errante, puta a Spiritu Sancto. Verum an ista corporalis speciositas Christi fuerit simpliciter major, quam aliqua unquam alterius hominis speciositas fuerit, de hoc diversimode dicitur. Ego autem pie credo quod Dominus meus Jesus Christus, etiam quantum ad corporalem pulchritudinem, ceteros omnes, imo et Absalonem excesserit, propter rationes prædictas. Non tamen semper (ut arbitror) æque pulcher in vultu apparuit, quoniam ea quæ pulchritudinem corporalem ornant atque conservant, non curavit, sed sprevit. Pulchritudo autem ejus spiritualis semper æqualis fuit, quia in gratia non profecit. Pulchritudo vero corporis sui, tempore passionis in tantum evanuit, ut de ipso ab Isaia dictum sit : Non est ei species, neque decor ; et vidimus eum, et non erat ei adspectus. De hac autem multiplici pulchritudine Sponsi cœlestis ac regis Messiæ, ait Sponsa : Dilectus meus candidus et rubicundus, electus ex millibus ; et, Ecce tu pulcher es, dilecte mi, et decorus. Sic ergo, o Christe, tu speciosus es forma præ filiis hominum. Quod enim id ipsum ad litteram de Christo dicatur, patet ex translatione Chaldaica, apud Hebræos authentica, quæ sic habet : Pulchritudo tua, rex Messia, major quam filiorum hominum.
paras.en: The third beauty of Christ was created and bodily, which consists in the due proportion, position and size of the members, and in a fitting overspreading of lively colour. And this beauty of Christ was great and striking. First, because no natural perfection was lacking to him. Second, because it was fitting that that most holy and most beautiful soul should receive a body proportioned to it, that is, beautiful and bright. Third, because the body of Christ was taken from the purest matter, namely from the most pure blood of the most worthy Virgin. Fourth, because it was formed and put together by an agent that cannot fail or err, that is, by the Holy Ghost. But whether this bodily beauty of Christ was simply greater than any beauty of any other man ever was, on this different things are said. I for my part piously believe that my Lord Jesus Christ, even in bodily beauty, surpassed all others, even Absalom[[2 Kings 14:25||]], for the reasons given. Yet he did not always (as I think) appear equally beautiful in face, since he did not care for the things that adorn and preserve bodily beauty, but despised them. His spiritual beauty, however, was always the same, because he did not advance in grace. But the beauty of his body so faded at the time of his passion that it was said of him by Isaias: [[Is 53:2|there is no beauty in him, nor comeliness: and we have seen him, and there was no sightliness|Non est ei species, neque decor ; et vidimus eum, et non erat ei adspectus]]. And of this manifold beauty of the heavenly Bridegroom and king Messias the Bride says: [[Cant 5:10|My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen out of thousands|Dilectus meus candidus et rubicundus, electus ex millibus]]; and, [[Cant 1:15|Behold thou art fair, my beloved, and comely|Ecce tu pulcher es, dilecte mi, et decorus]]. So then, O Christ, [[44:3|thou art beautiful above the sons of men|tu speciosus es forma præ filiis hominum]]. For that this very thing is said literally of Christ is clear from the Chaldee translation, held authoritative among the Hebrews, which reads thus: Thy beauty, O king Messias, is greater than that of the sons of men.

paras.t: Porro in libris annalibus Romanorum legitur, quod Christus fuit staturæ proceræ, mediocris et spectabilis, vultum habens venerabilem, quem possent intuentes diligere et formidare ; capillos habens coloris nucis avellanæ præmaturæ, planos fere usque ad aures, ab auribus cincinnos crispos aliquantulum cæruliores et fulgentiores, ab humeris ventilantes ; discrimen habens in medio capitis juxta morem Nazaræorum, frontem planam ac serenissimam sine macula ac ruga, quam rubor moderatus venustavit ; nasi et oris nulla prorsus reprehensio : barbam habens copiosam, capillis concolorem, non longam, sed in mento parum bifurcatam, adspectum simplicem et maturum, oculis glaucis, variis et claris exsistentibus ; in increpatione terribilis, in admonitione blandus et amabilis, hilaris servata gravitate : aliquando flevit, sed nunquam risit ; statura corporis propagatus et rectus, brachia vero et manus visui delectabiles, alloquio gravis, rarus et modestus : talis utique per omnia, ut merito diceretur, Speciosus forma præ filiis hominum.
paras.en: Moreover, it is read in the annals of the Romans that Christ was of tall stature, of middling build and comely to look on, having a venerable face, such that those who looked on it could both love and fear him; having hair of the colour of a hazelnut fully ripe, smooth almost down to the ears, and from the ears in curling locks somewhat darker and more shining, waving about from the shoulders; having a parting in the middle of the head after the manner of the Nazarenes; a forehead smooth and most serene, without spot or wrinkle, graced by a moderate ruddiness; nose and mouth altogether faultless; having a full beard of the colour of his hair, not long, but a little forked at the chin; a simple and mature look, the eyes grey, changeful and clear; terrible in rebuke, gentle and lovable in admonition, cheerful while keeping his gravity; he sometimes wept, but never laughed; in stature of body tall and straight, his arms and hands a delight to see; in speech grave, sparing and modest: such indeed in all things that he might rightly be called: [[44:3|Thou art beautiful above the sons of men|Speciosus forma præ filiis hominum]] [a footnote of the edition says that earlier editions inserted here the letters of Lentulus and Pilate about Christ, which, according to the edition of 1558, are not found in the Author's original].

paras.t: Deinde Christus laudatur ab eloquentia. Diffusa est gratia in labiis tuis : id est, fructuosa et efficax eloquentia data est tibi. Unde per Isaiam Christus ait : Posuit Dominus os meum quasi gladium acutum. Et ipsi quoque adversarii Christi, compulsi sunt dicere : Nunquam sic locutus est homo, sicut hic loquitur. Sed et de ipso apud Lucam legitur : Mirabantur omnes in verbis gratiæ quæ procedebant de ore ejus. Efficaciam autem Christi in loquendo pandit Evangelista dum ait : Erat docens sicut virtutem habens, non sicut Pharisæi et Scribæ. Sciendum quoque, quod Christus habuit donum linguarum, sicut et ceteras gratias gratis datas : non tamen legitur usus hoc dono, quia non prædicavit nisi in Hebræo. Unde ipse ait : Non sum missus nisi ad oves quæ perierunt domus Israel. Denique, sicut manus est organum intellectus practici, sic lingua est organum seu instrumentum intellectus speculativi. Quemadmodum ergo Christus habuit summam sapientiam, sic decuit eum habere summam eloquentiam. Ideo de gratia labiorum Christi sponsi sui ait Sponsa : Anima mea liquefacta est, ut dilectus locutus est.
paras.en: Then Christ is praised for his eloquence. [[44:3|grace is poured abroad in thy lips|Diffusa est gratia in labiis tuis]]: that is, a fruitful and effective eloquence has been given thee. Hence Christ says through Isaias: The Lord [[Is 49:2|hath made my mouth like a sharp sword|Posuit Dominus os meum quasi gladium acutum]]. And even Christ's adversaries were compelled to say: [[John 7:46|Never did man speak like this man|Nunquam sic locutus est homo, sicut hic loquitur]]. And in Luke too it is read of him that all [[Luke 4:22|wondered at the words of grace that proceeded from his mouth|Mirabantur omnes in verbis gratiæ quæ procedebant de ore ejus]]. And the Evangelist shows Christ's effectiveness in speaking when he says: [[Matt 7:29|he was teaching them as one having power, and not as the scribes and Pharisees|Erat docens sicut virtutem habens, non sicut Pharisæi et Scribæ]]. It should also be known that Christ had the gift of tongues, as he had the other graces freely given [*gratiæ gratis datæ*: gifts such as prophecy and tongues, given for the good of others rather than for the holiness of the one who has them]; yet we do not read that he used this gift, because he preached only in Hebrew. Hence he himself says: [[Matt 15:24|I was not sent but to the sheep, that are lost of the house of Israel|Non sum missus nisi ad oves quæ perierunt domus Israel]]. Lastly, as the hand is the organ of the practical intellect, so the tongue is the organ or instrument of the speculative intellect. As Christ, then, had the highest wisdom, so it was fitting that he should have the highest eloquence. Therefore the Bride says of the grace of the lips of Christ her Bridegroom: [[Cant 5:6|My soul melted when he spoke|Anima mea liquefacta est, ut dilectus locutus est]].

paras.t: Propterea benedixit te Deus in æternum. Benedictio Dei, est collatio seu infusio gratiæ Dei ac divinorum donorum, et multiplicatio eorumdem. Christus autem in gratia non profecit, nec sibi ipsi aliquid de essentiali præmio meruit, sicut ubertim præhabitum est. Quomodo ergo propter gratiam labiorum suorum benedictus a Deo asseritur? Et respondendum, quod benedictio ista intelligenda est quantum ad accidentale præmium Christi. Nam per prædicationem suam sanctissimam meruit sibi corporis sui glorificationem et ascensionem. Potest quoque benedictio ista referri ad fructum eloquentiæ Christi, atque ad mysticum corpus ipsius. Dicimus enim terram seu arborem benedici, dum fert copiosum fructum. Similiter quoniam per Christi doctrinam multi salutem sortiti sunt, ipse Christus ratione suæ eloquentiæ benedici asseritur.
paras.en: [[44:3|therefore hath God blessed thee for ever|Propterea benedixit te Deus in æternum]]. The blessing of God is the bestowal or infusion of the grace of God and of divine gifts, and the multiplying of them. But Christ did not advance in grace, nor did he merit for himself anything of the essential reward, as has been set out at length before. How then is he said to be blessed by God because of the grace of his lips? The answer is that this blessing is to be understood with regard to Christ's accidental reward [the joys added to the essential reward, which is the vision of God; for Christ, such as the glory of his body]. For by his most holy preaching he merited for himself the glorification of his body and his ascension. This blessing can also be referred to the fruit of Christ's eloquence, and to his mystical body. For we say that land or a tree is blessed when it bears abundant fruit. Likewise, since many have obtained salvation through Christ's teaching, Christ himself is said to be blessed by reason of his eloquence.

paras.t: Accingere gladio tuo super femur tuum, potentissime : id est, o rex Christe, qui es salvator omnipotens et debellator aeriarum potestatum fortissimus, accingere, id est, te ipsum accinge, vel a tota Trinitate accingaris, gladio tuo, id est prædicatione divina, verbo Dei, sermone justitiæ, ita ut gratiam in labiis tuis diffusam effundas, eaque ad mundi informationem utaris : accingere, inquam, super femur tuum, id est super intellectum tuum, ita ut sapienter loquaris, et efficaciter doceas. Bene equidem per gladium intelligitur verbum Dei seu prædicatio Evangelii, juxta illud divini Apostoli : In omnibus sumentes scutum fidei, et gladium spiritus, quod est verbum Dei. Et iterum : Vivus est, inquit, sermo Dei et efficax, et penetrabilior omni gladio ancipiti. Dicitur enim verbum Dei gladius ratione sui effectus, quoniam intima mentis penetrat, peccata occidit, dæmonemque exsuperat. Unde ad Jeremiam Dominus ait : Numquid non verba mea sunt quasi ignis, et quasi malleus conterens petram? Et Ecclesiastes ait : Verba sapientium sicut stimuli, et quasi clavi in altum defixi.
paras.en: [[44:4|Gird thy sword upon thy thigh, O thou most mighty|Accingere gladio tuo super femur tuum, potentissime]]: that is, O king Christ, who art the almighty Saviour and the mightiest vanquisher of the powers of the air, [[44:4|gird|accingere]], that is, gird thyself, or be girded by the whole Trinity, with [[44:4|thy sword|gladio tuo]], that is, with divine preaching, the word of God, the speech of justice, so that thou mayest pour out the grace poured abroad in thy lips, and use it for the instruction of the world: [[44:4|gird|accingere]], I say, [[44:4|upon thy thigh|super femur tuum]], that is, upon thy intellect, so that thou mayest speak wisely and teach effectively. Rightly indeed is the word of God, or the preaching of the Gospel, understood by the sword, according to that saying of the divine Apostle: [[Eph 6:16|In all things taking the shield of faith|In omnibus sumentes scutum fidei]], and [[Eph 6:17|the sword of the Spirit (which is the word of God)|gladium spiritus, quod est verbum Dei]]. And again: [[Heb 4:12|the word of God is living|Vivus est]], he says, [[Heb 4:12|and effectual and more piercing than any two edged sword|sermo Dei et efficax, et penetrabilior omni gladio ancipiti]]. For the word of God is called a sword by reason of its effect, since it pierces the inmost parts of the mind, slays sins, and overcomes the devil. Hence the Lord says to Jeremias: [[Jer 23:29|Are not my words as a fire|Numquid non verba mea sunt quasi ignis]], [[Jer 23:29|and as a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?|et quasi malleus conterens petram]] And Ecclesiastes says: [[Eccles 12:11|The words of the wise are as goads, and as nails deeply fastened in|Verba sapientium sicut stimuli, et quasi clavi in altum defixi]].

paras.t: Convenienter quoque per femur accipitur intellectus. Quemadmodum enim femur corporis est seminarium generationis, secundum illud, Non auferetur sceptrum de Juda, et dux de femore ejus, donec veniat qui mittendus est ; sic intellectus est seminarium spiritualis procreationis. Nam ut Christus in Evangelio asserit, Semen est verbum Dei. Verbum autem ab intellectu procedit, sicut ait Philosophus. Sunt ergo ea quæ sunt in voce, earum quæ sunt in animo passionum notæ. Intellectus itaque per verbum oris spiritualiter generat, prout ad Galatas dicit Apostolus : Filioli mei, quos iterum parturio, donec formetur Christus in vobis. De hoc femore intellectuali, cui supercingitur gladius verbi, ait Jeremias : Converte me, Domine, et convertar. Postquam enim convertisti me, egi pœnitentiam ; et postquam ostendisti mihi, percussi femur meum.
paras.en: Fittingly also the intellect is understood by the thigh. For as the thigh of the body is the seed-bed of generation, according to that saying, [[Gen 49:10|The sceptre shall not be taken away from Juda, nor a ruler from his thigh, till he come that is to be sent|Non auferetur sceptrum de Juda, et dux de femore ejus, donec veniat qui mittendus est]], so the intellect is the seed-bed of spiritual begetting. For, as Christ declares in the Gospel, [[Luke 8:11|The seed is the word of God|Semen est verbum Dei]]. And the word proceeds from the intellect, as the Philosopher says: the things that are in the voice are signs of the passions that are in the soul [Aristotle, *On Interpretation*, ch. 1: spoken words are signs of what the mind undergoes]. The intellect, then, begets spiritually through the word of the mouth, as the Apostle says to the Galatians: [[Gal 4:19|My little children, of whom I am in labour again, until Christ be formed in you.|Filioli mei, quos iterum parturio, donec formetur Christus in vobis]] Of this thigh of the intellect, upon which the sword of the word is girded, Jeremias says: [[Jer 31:18|Convert me|Converte me]], O Lord, [[Jer 31:18|and I shall be converted|et convertar]]. [[Jer 31:19|For after thou didst convert me, I did penance: and after thou didst shew unto me, I struck my thigh|Postquam enim convertisti me, egi pœnitentiam ; et postquam ostendisti mihi, percussi femur meum]].

paras.t: De potentia autem Christi, in præcedentis psalmi elucidatione multa inducta sunt : quibus hoc adjici potest, quod apud Michæam de ea commemoratur : Exaltabitur manus tua super hostes tuos ; et omnes inimici tui interibunt. Et Apostolus de Christo loquens : Quum sit, inquit, splendor gloriæ, portansque omnia verbo virtutis suæ. Unde Christus Dei sapientia inquit : Omnium excellentium et sublimium colla calcavi.
paras.en: Of the power of Christ [the *potentissime*, "O thou most mighty", of the verse] much was brought forward in the explanation of the preceding psalm; to which this may be added, which is recorded of it in Micheas: [[Mich 5:9|Thy hand shall be lifted up over thy enemies, and all thy enemies shall be cut off.|Exaltabitur manus tua super hostes tuos ; et omnes inimici tui interibunt]] And the Apostle, speaking of Christ: [[Heb 1:3|being|Quum sit]], he says, [[Heb 1:3|the brightness of his glory|splendor gloriæ]], [[Heb 1:3|upholding all things by the word of his power|portansque omnia verbo virtutis suæ]]. Hence Christ, the wisdom of God, says: [[Ecclus 24:11|I have trodden under my feet the hearts of all the high and low|Omnium excellentium et sublimium colla calcavi]] [Denis reads "I have trodden on the necks of all the high and lofty"; the Vulgate has "by my power I have trodden on the hearts of all the high and low"].

paras.t: Specie tua creata, et pulchritudine tua increata, intende prospere, id est, feliciter respice, et ad nostram æternam prosperitatem pie considera genus humanum, ut illud salvifices ; procede de sinu Patris in uterum Virginis, de cœlo summo in inferiores partes terræ, de utero Matris in præsepe, de præsepi in publicum, deinde in crucem, et tandem in cœlum. Sic ergo procede, quemadmodum Sponsa ait : Ecce iste venit saliens in montibus, transiliens colles. Et regna in militanti Ecclesia per fidem et gratiam, atque in triumphanti Ecclesia per visionem beatam. Itaque, o Christe, regna, quatenus impleatur illud, In die illa erit Dominus rex super omnem terram ; et illud, Erit Domino regnum. De hoc Christi regno etiam ait Apostolus : Deus exaltavit illum, et dedit illi nomen quod est super omne nomen, ut in nomine Jesu omne genu flectatur, cœlestium et terrestrium et infernorum. Et iterum : Deus, inquit, constituit illum ad dexteram suam in cœlestibus, super omnem principatum et potestatem et virtutem et dominationem. Propter quod in Evangelio etiam Christus affirmat : Data est mihi omnis potestas in cœlo et in terra.
paras.en: [[44:5|With thy comeliness|Specie tua]] that is created, [[44:5|and thy beauty|et pulchritudine tua]] that is uncreated, [[44:5|set out|intende]] [[44:5|prosperously|prospere]] [Denis takes *prospere*, "prosperously", with *intende*, "set out" (literally "look" or "attend"), not with *procede*]: that is, look upon us favourably, and with mercy regard the human race for our eternal prosperity, that thou mayest save it; [[44:5|proceed|procede]] from the bosom of the Father into the womb of the Virgin, from the highest heaven into the lower parts of the earth, from the womb of thy Mother into the manger, from the manger into public life, then onto the cross, and at last into heaven. So then proceed, as the Bride says: [[Cant 2:8|behold he cometh leaping upon the mountains, skipping over the hills|Ecce iste venit saliens in montibus, transiliens colles]]. [[44:5|and reign|Et regna]] in the Church militant by faith and grace, and in the Church triumphant by the blessed vision. Reign, therefore, O Christ, that this may be fulfilled: [[Zach 14:9|in that day|In die illa]] [[Zach 14:9|the Lord shall be king over all the earth|erit Dominus rex super omnem terram]] [Denis sets "in that day", from later in the verse, at its head; the margin gives Zach. xiv, 8, 9]; and this: [[Abd 1:21|the kingdom shall be for the Lord|Erit Domino regnum]]. Of this kingdom of Christ the Apostle also says: [[Phil 2:9|God also hath exalted him and hath given him a name which is above all names|Deus exaltavit illum, et dedit illi nomen quod est super omne nomen]], [[Phil 2:10|That in the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those that are in heaven, on earth, and under the earth|ut in nomine Jesu omne genu flectatur, cœlestium et terrestrium et infernorum]]. And again he speaks of God [[Eph 1:20|setting him on his right hand in the heavenly places|constituit illum ad dexteram suam in cœlestibus]], [[Eph 1:21|Above all principality and power and virtue and dominion|super omnem principatum et potestatem et virtutem et dominationem]]. Wherefore Christ too declares in the Gospel: [[Matt 28:18|All power is given to me in heaven and in earth|Data est mihi omnis potestas in cœlo et in terra]].

paras.t: Considerandum autem, quod Christus hoc dixit post resurrectionem suam : sed non est hoc ita intelligendum, quasi tunc primum data sit Christo homini prædicta potestas ; imo a primo suæ humanæ conceptionis instanti, data est ei omnis potestas in cœlo et in terra. Nam eo ipso quo Christi humana natura unita est Deo unione personali, subjecta est ei omnis creatura. Ideoque Baptista de Christo ante passionem ejus dixit : Pater diligit Filium, et omnia dedit in manu ejus. Et Christus ait : Quæcumque facit Pater, hæc et Filius similiter facit. Et in hoc Christus insinuat unam atque eamdem essentiam et potentiam sui ac Patris, quia a diversis seu distinctis suppositis emanare non potest operatio eadem numero, nisi in natura et potestate conveniant : imo in verbis his fatetur se Christus verum Deum. Nisi enim esset verus Deus, ipse non faceret quæ facit Pater, similiter Patri, vel similiter sicut Pater. Nam si pura creatura esset, ut Ariani mentiti sunt, Pater faceret principaliter, et Filius instrumentaliter.
paras.en: But it should be considered that Christ said this after his resurrection; yet it is not to be understood as though the said power was then first given to Christ as man: rather, from the first instant of his human conception all power in heaven and on earth was given to him. For by the very fact that Christ's human nature was united to God in personal union, every creature was made subject to it. And therefore the Baptist said of Christ before his passion: [[John 3:35|The Father loveth the Son: and he hath given all things into his hand.|Pater diligit Filium, et omnia dedit in manu ejus]] And Christ says: [[John 5:19|what things soever he doth, these the Son also doth in like manner|Quæcumque facit Pater, hæc et Filius similiter facit]]. And in this Christ suggests that he and the Father have one and the same essence and power, since one and the same operation in number cannot come from different or distinct supposits [that is, distinct subsisting beings] unless they agree in nature and power: indeed in these words Christ confesses himself true God. For unless he were true God, he would not do what the Father does in like manner with the Father, or in like manner as the Father. For if he were a mere creature, as the Arians falsely said, the Father would act as principal cause and the Son as an instrument.

paras.t: Propter veritatem et mansuetudinem et justitiam : id est, quia in veritate et mansuetudine atque justitia confirmatus fuisti, o Christe, ex utero matris ; idcirco et deducet te mirabiliter, id est, in omni conversatione tua sine culpa, et omnino irreprehensibiliter diriget te dextera tua, id est divina tua natura, quæ tua humanitate dignior atque robustior est, sicut dextera nobilior potentiorque consistit quam sinistra. Christus enim sine omni peccato inter homines conversatus est : quod utique super hominem est, et mirabile nimis, præsertim quum justus septies cadat in die.
paras.en: [[44:5|Because of truth and meekness and justice|Propter veritatem et mansuetudinem et justitiam]]: that is, because thou wast confirmed in truth and meekness and justice, O Christ, from thy mother's womb, therefore [[44:5|shall conduct thee wonderfully|et deducet te mirabiliter]], that is, shall guide thee in all thy conduct without fault and altogether blamelessly, [[44:5|thy right hand|dextera tua]], that is, thy divine nature, which is worthier and stronger than thy humanity, as the right hand is nobler and more powerful than the left. For Christ lived among men without any sin: which is surely above man and exceedingly wonderful, especially since [[Prov 24:16|a just man shall fall seven times|justus septies cadat]] in a day [Denis adds "in a day", as the saying is commonly quoted; the verse itself does not have it].

paras.t: Vel sic : Propter veritatem et mansuetudinem et justitiam, id est propter actus harum virtutum et merito earum, videlicet quia vita et doctrina verus fuisti, et in adversis mitis ac patiens, atque in omnibus justus, non propriam, sed Patris gloriam, hominumque salutem quærens ; propterea deducet te mirabiliter dextera tua, videlicet elevans te de terra ad cœlos, et statuens te judicem universorum. Ascensionem enim et judiciariam potestatem Christus sua exinanitione et sancta conversatione promeruit. Christus enim in omnibus veritatem dixit et observavit, secundum quod ipse coram Pilato testatus est : Ego in hoc natus sum, et ad hoc veni in mundum, ut testimonium perhibeam veritati. Erat etiam mansuetus, quemadmodum ait : Discite a me quia mitis sum et humilis. Erat et justus, sicut ad Judæos Stephanus ait : Quem Prophetarum non sunt persecuti patres vestri? Et occiderunt eos qui prænuntiaverunt de adventu Justi, cujus vos nunc proditores et homicidæ fuistis.
paras.en: Or thus: [[44:5|Because of truth and meekness and justice|Propter veritatem et mansuetudinem et justitiam]], that is, because of the acts of these virtues and by their merit, namely because thou wast true in life and teaching, meek and patient in adversity, and just in all things, seeking not thy own glory but the Father's, and the salvation of men; therefore [[44:5|thy right hand shall conduct thee wonderfully|deducet te mirabiliter dextera tua]], namely by raising thee from earth to heaven and appointing thee judge of all. For Christ merited his ascension and his power of judgement by his self-emptying [*exinanitio*, the "emptying" of himself of which the Apostle speaks] and his holy life. For Christ spoke and kept the truth in all things, as he himself testified before Pilate: [[John 18:37|For this was I born, and for this came I into the world; that I should give testimony to the truth|Ego in hoc natus sum, et ad hoc veni in mundum, ut testimonium perhibeam veritati]]. He was also meek, as he says: [[Matt 11:29|learn of me, because I am meek, and humble|Discite a me quia mitis sum et humilis]]. He was also just, as Stephen says to the Jews: [[Acts 7:52|Which of the prophets have not your fathers persecuted? And they have slain them who foretold of the coming of the Just One: of whom you have been now the betrayers and murderers|Quem Prophetarum non sunt persecuti patres vestri? Et occiderunt eos qui prænuntiaverunt de adventu Justi, cujus vos nunc proditores et homicidæ fuistis]].

paras.t: Sagittæ tuæ acutæ: id est, verba prædicationis tuæ, o Christe, sunt penetrativa cordis, et interiora animæ expurgantia, atque timorem salubrem incutientia; populi sub te cadent: id est, infideles qui ante tibi inobedientes rebellesque fuerant, audita prædicatione tua ac discipulorum tuorum, convertentur ad fidem, et tibi obedient. Cadent autem sub te in corde, id est in medio, inimicorum regis, id est gentilium qui erant hostes tui, qui es rex summus et verus. In toto enim mundo ceciderunt spiritualiter, id est, Christo per fidem subjecti sunt, qui tempore incredulitatis inimici exstiterant. Unde Apostolus ait: Commendat autem caritatem suam Deus in nobis, quoniam quum adhuc inimici essemus, ille pro nobis mortuus est. Et: Christus est pax nostra, qui fecit utraque unum, per crucem dissolvens inimicitias in semetipso. Cui consonat quod de Christo prædictum est: Et erit iste pax Assyriis, quum venerit in terram nostram, et quando calcaverit in domibus nostris. Huic autem expositioni concordat quod infra de Christo habetur, Dominare in medio inimicorum tuorum; id quoque quod ait Michæas, Convertentur (ad ipsum), quia nunc magnificabitur in medio universæ terræ. De hoc autem casu populorum sub Christo et regno ejus super inimicos suos, pulcherrime vaticinatus est Daniel: Suscitabit, inquiens, Deus cœli regnum, quod in æternum non dissipabitur; secundum quod vidisti, quod de monte abscissus est lapis sine manibus, et comminuit testam et ferrum et æs et argentum et aurum. Lapis enim abscissus de monte sine manibus, est Christus, natus de Virgine sine viri seminibus: et hic lapis comminuit prædicta metalla, per quæ designantur mundi regna, dum Apostoli virtute Christi ad fidem atque obsequium ejus universum mundum converterunt, idololatriam exstirpantes. Et hoc est quod a Sophonia inducitur: Horribilis Dominus super impios, et attenuabit omnes deos terræ, et adorabunt eum viri de loco suo, omnes insulæ gentium. Propter quod rursus ait Propheta: Idola penitus conterentur. Vel sic: Populi sub te cadent in corde, id est, casus iste erit spiritualis per obedientiam mentis, non corporalis.
paras.en: [[44:6|Thy arrows are sharp|Sagittæ tuæ acutæ]]: that is, the words of thy preaching, O Christ, pierce the heart, purge the inmost parts of the soul and strike a wholesome fear into it; [[44:6|under thee shall people fall|populi sub te cadent]]: that is, the unbelievers, who before were disobedient and rebellious towards thee, shall be converted to the faith when they have heard the preaching of thee and of thy disciples, and shall obey thee. And they shall fall under thee [[44:6|into the hearts|in corde]] [Denis reads *in corde*, "in the heart", which he takes as "in the midst"; the Vulgate has *in corda*, "into the hearts"], that is, in the midst, [[44:6|of the king's enemies|inimicorum regis]], that is, of the Gentiles, who were enemies of thee, who art the highest and true king. For throughout the whole world they fell spiritually: that is, those who in the time of their unbelief had been enemies were made subject to Christ by faith. Hence the Apostle says: [[Rom 5:8|But God commendeth his charity towards us: because when as yet we were|Commendat autem caritatem suam Deus in nobis, quoniam quum adhuc]] enemies [Denis has *inimici*, "enemies", as in Rom 5:10; here the Apostle has *peccatores*, "sinners"], [[Rom 5:9|Christ died for us|ille pro nobis mortuus est]]. And: Christ [[Eph 2:14|is our peace, who hath made both one|est pax nostra, qui fecit utraque unum]], [[Eph 2:16|by the cross, killing the enmities in himself|per crucem dissolvens inimicitias in semetipso]]. With this agrees what was foretold of Christ: [[Mich 5:5|And this man shall be our peace, when the Assyrian shall come into our land, and when he shall set his foot in our houses|Et erit iste pax Assyriis, quum venerit in terram nostram, et quando calcaverit in domibus nostris]] [Denis reads *pax Assyriis*, "peace to the Assyrians", where the Vulgate has *pax: cum venerit Assyrius*, "peace, when the Assyrian shall come"]. And with this explanation accords what is found further on concerning Christ: [[Ps 109:2|rule thou in the midst of thy enemies|Dominare in medio inimicorum tuorum]]; and also what Micheas says: [[Mich 5:4|they shall be converted|Convertentur]] (to him), [[Mich 5:4|for now shall he be magnified|quia nunc magnificabitur]] in the midst of the whole earth [the Vulgate has *usque ad terminos terræ*, "even to the ends of the earth"]. Of this falling of the peoples under Christ, and of his kingdom over his enemies, Daniel prophesied most beautifully: [[Dan 2:44|the God of heaven|Deus cœli]] [[Dan 2:44|will set up|Suscitabit]], he says, [[Dan 2:44|a kingdom that shall never be destroyed|regnum, quod in æternum non dissipabitur]]; [[Dan 2:45|According as thou sawest, that the stone was cut out of the mountain without hands, and broke in pieces the clay and the iron, and the brass, and the silver, and the gold|secundum quod vidisti, quod de monte abscissus est lapis sine manibus, et comminuit testam et ferrum et æs et argentum et aurum]]. For the stone cut out of the mountain without hands is Christ, born of the Virgin without the seed of man; and this stone broke in pieces the metals named, by which the kingdoms of the world are signified, when the Apostles, by the power of Christ, converted the whole world to faith in him and to his service, rooting out idolatry. And this is what Sophonias brings in: [[Soph 2:11|The Lord shall be terrible upon them, and shall consume all the gods of the earth: and they shall adore him every man from his own place, all the islands of the Gentiles|Horribilis Dominus super impios, et attenuabit omnes deos terræ, et adorabunt eum viri de loco suo, omnes insulæ gentium]] [for "upon them" Denis has *super impios*, "upon the wicked"]. For which reason the Prophet says again: [[Is 2:18|idols shall be utterly destroyed|Idola penitus conterentur]]. Or thus: [[44:6|under thee shall people fall|Populi sub te cadent]] [[44:6|into the hearts|in corde]]: that is, this fall will be spiritual, by the obedience of the mind, not bodily.

paras.t: Sedes tua, Deus, in sæculum sæculi: id est, thronus gloriæ tuæ atque judiciaria tua potestas, o Christe, qui es Deus verus, æternaliter stabit, nec unquam deficiet: quemadmodum ab alio dictum est, Potestas ejus, potestas æterna, quæ non auferetur, et regnum ejus quod non corrumpetur; et per alium, Ipse portabit gloriam, et sedebit et dominabitur in solio suo.
paras.en: [[44:7|Thy throne, O God, is forever and ever|Sedes tua, Deus, in sæculum sæculi]]: that is, the throne of thy glory and thy power of judgment, O Christ, who art true God, shall stand eternally and shall never fail; as was said by one prophet: [[Dan 7:14|his power is an everlasting power that shall not be taken away: and his kingdom that shall not be destroyed|Potestas ejus, potestas æterna, quæ non auferetur, et regnum ejus quod non corrumpetur]]; and by another: [[Zach 6:13|he shall bear the glory, and shall sit, and rule upon his throne|Ipse portabit gloriam, et sedebit et dominabitur in solio suo]].

paras.t: Virga directionis, virga regni tui: id est, lex seu doctrina tua, quæ est virga regni tui, id est Ecclesiæ, per quam ipsa fideles regit et judicat, est virga directionis, id est justa directio et rectum judicium, quia neminem palpat, et personam non accipit. Christus enim præfixit Ecclesiæ suæ justitiæ regulas, per quas dirigit Christianos. De hac virga Christi Isaias ait: Percutiet terram virga oris sui, et spiritu labiorum suorum interficiet impium. Vel sic: Virga regni tui, id est ipsum regimen tuum, quo regis et judicas Ecclesiam, quæ est regnum tuum, est virga directionis, id est justa correctio, æqua retributio, et gubernatio omnium directiva. Christus namque in se ipso justus est judex, et singula rectissime atque justissime dirigit. Unde de hac virga Christi judiciaria apud Isaiam legitur: Non secundum visionem oculorum judicabit, neque secundum auditum aurium arguet; sed judicabit in justitia pauperes, et arguet in æquitate pro mansuetis terræ. Unde et Christus in Evangelio ait: Nolite secundum faciem judicare. Sed et de virga hac regiminis Christi apud Jeremiam dicitur: Regnabit rex et sapiens erit, et faciet judicium et justitiam in terra.
paras.en: [[44:7|the sceptre of thy kingdom is a sceptre of uprightness|Virga directionis, virga regni tui]] [*virga* is both "sceptre" and "rod"; *directio*, "uprightness", is literally "direction", right guiding: Denis plays on both words below]: that is, thy law or doctrine, which is the sceptre of thy kingdom, that is, of the Church, by which she rules and judges the faithful, is a sceptre of uprightness, that is, just direction and right judgment, for it flatters no one and is no respecter of persons. For Christ has set before his Church rules of justice, by which he directs Christians. Of this rod of Christ Isaias says: [[Is 11:4|he shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall slay the wicked|Percutiet terram virga oris sui, et spiritu labiorum suorum interficiet impium]]. Or thus: [[44:7|the sceptre of thy kingdom|Virga regni tui]], that is, thy very rule, by which thou rulest and judgest the Church, which is thy kingdom, [[44:7|is a sceptre of uprightness|est virga directionis]], that is, just correction, fair retribution, and a governance that directs all things aright. For Christ in himself is a just judge, and directs each thing most rightly and most justly. Hence of this judicial rod of Christ we read in Isaias: [[Is 11:3|He shall not judge according to the sight of the eyes, nor reprove according to the hearing of the ears|Non secundum visionem oculorum judicabit, neque secundum auditum aurium arguet]]; [[Is 11:4|But he shall judge the poor with justice, and shall reprove with equity the meek of the earth|sed judicabit in justitia pauperes, et arguet in æquitate pro mansuetis terræ]]. Hence Christ too says in the Gospel: [[John 7:24|Judge not according to the appearance|Nolite secundum faciem judicare]]. And of this rod of Christ's rule it is said in Jeremias: [[Jer 23:5|a king shall reign, and shall be wise: and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth|Regnabit rex et sapiens erit, et faciet judicium et justitiam in terra]].

paras.t: Hunc autem versiculum cum sequenti allegat Apostolus ad Hebræos de Christo prædictum. Unde liquet psalmum istum ad litteram esse de Christo conscriptum. Postremo diligentissime advertendum, quod sanctus Propheta in versu hoc aperte insinuat Christum esse Deum. Nam de eodem de quo prædixit, Speciosus forma præ filiis hominum, etc., usque ad hunc versum: de eo nunc addit, Sedes tua, Deus, in sæculum sæculi. Et quod hoc de Christo dicatur, evidentissime patet ex eo quod protinus de eodem, de quo prælocutus est, subdit:
paras.en: Now the Apostle, in the Epistle to the Hebrews, cites this verse together with the next as foretold of Christ[[Heb 1:8||]][[Heb 1:9||]]. Hence it is clear that this psalm was written, according to the letter, about Christ. Lastly, it must be noted most carefully that in this verse the holy Prophet plainly intimates that Christ is God. For of the same one of whom he said before, [[44:3|Thou art beautiful above the sons of men|Speciosus forma præ filiis hominum]], etc., up to this verse, of him he now adds: [[44:7|Thy throne, O God, is forever and ever|Sedes tua, Deus, in sæculum sæculi]]. And that this is said of Christ is most evidently plain from this, that straight after, of the same one of whom he has been speaking, he adds:

paras.t: Dilexisti justitiam, et odisti iniquitatem: propterea unxit te Deus. Hoc enim de Deo secundum naturam divinam non dicitur, quia secundum eam unctus non est: de Deo igitur incarnato ista dicuntur. Quamvis enim Christo secundum utramque naturam conveniat diligere justitiam, odioque habere iniquitatem; tamen præsenti loco ista dicuntur de Christo secundum humanitatem assumptam, quia subjungit, Propterea unxit te Deus. In præcedenti versu vocavit Christum Deum, nunc dicit eum unctum a Deo. Innuit ergo personalem esse distinctionem in Deo; et est sensus: Quia, o Christe, dilexisti justitiam, et odisti iniquitatem, propterea unxit te Deus omnium, Deus tuus singularissimo modo, oleo lætitiæ, id est gloria resurrectionis et ascensionis accidentalique præmio, præ consortibus tuis, id est prius et plenius quam alios homines, quoniam tu es primogenitus ex mortuis.
paras.en: [[44:8|Thou hast loved justice, and hated iniquity|Dilexisti justitiam, et odisti iniquitatem]]: [[44:8|therefore God|propterea]] [[44:8|hath anointed thee|unxit te Deus]]. For this is not said of God according to the divine nature, since according to that he was not anointed: these things, then, are said of God incarnate. For although it befits Christ according to each nature to love justice and to hate iniquity, yet in the present place these things are said of Christ according to the humanity he assumed, since he goes on: [[44:8|therefore God|Propterea]] [[44:8|hath anointed thee|unxit te Deus]]. In the preceding verse he called Christ God; now he says that he was anointed by God. He therefore intimates that there is a distinction of persons in God. And the sense is: Because, O Christ, thou hast loved justice and hated iniquity, therefore the God of all, [[44:8|thy God|Deus tuus]] in a most singular way, hath anointed thee [[44:8|with the oil of gladness|oleo lætitiæ]], that is, with the glory of the resurrection and the ascension and with the accidental reward [that is, the joy added to the essential reward, which is the vision of God], [[44:8|above thy fellows|præ consortibus tuis]], that is, sooner and more fully than other men, for thou art [[Col 1:18|the firstborn from the dead|primogenitus ex mortuis]].

paras.t: Alii aliter exponunt, dicentes: Propterea unxit te Deus, Deus tuus, oleo lætitiæ, id est dulcedine seu plenitudine gratiæ et conservatione ab omni peccato. Sed his obviare videtur, quod Christus a primo suæ conceptionis humanæ instanti, plenus erat omni virtute et gratia, nec aliquo modo meruit per actum præcedentem gratiæ infusionem. Posset tamen, ni fallor, dici ad hoc, quod ista vox, Propterea, non dicit causam, sed signum. Nam quod Christus dilexit justitiam, signum est quod Deus unxit eum oleo gratiæ, secundum quod ante inductum est: Prævenisti eum in benedictionibus dulcedinis. Et per Isaiam ipse Christus: Spiritus, inquit, Domini super me, eo quod unxerit me.
paras.en: Others explain it otherwise, saying: [[44:8|therefore God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness|Propterea unxit te Deus, Deus tuus, oleo lætitiæ]], that is, with the sweetness or fullness of grace and with preservation from all sin. But against these there seems to stand the fact that Christ, from the first instant of his human conception, was full of all virtue and grace, and in no way merited the infusion of grace by any act going before. Yet, unless I am mistaken, it could be said to this that the word "therefore" does not state a cause, but a sign. For that Christ loved justice is a sign that God anointed him with the oil of grace, as was brought in before: [[Ps 20:4|thou hast prevented him with blessings of sweetness|Prævenisti eum in benedictionibus dulcedinis]] [*prevented*, that is, gone before]. And Christ himself says through Isaias: [[Is 61:1|The spirit|Spiritus]], he says, [[Is 61:1|of the Lord is upon me, because the Lord hath anointed me|Domini super me, eo quod unxerit me]][[Luke 4:18||]].

paras.t: Myrrha et gutta et casia a vestimentis tuis, a domibus eburneis. Per myrrham, quæ amara est, et a putrefactione præservat cadavera, vermesque arcet, mortificatio carnis accipitur: quæ concupiscentiarum fœtores ac vitiorum squalores expellit, secundum quod ait Apostolus: Nihil damnationis est his qui sunt in Christo Jesu, qui non secundum carnem ambulant. Et iterum: Si secundum carnem vixeritis, moriemini; si autem spiritu facta carnis mortificaveritis, vivetis. Per guttam vero, quæ aromatica est, et inflaturas ac duritias tollit, humilitas designatur. Unde Salomon ait: Qui mentis est duræ, corruet in mala; sed humilem spiritu suscipiet gloria. Per casiam vero, quæ in locis humidis nascitur, et altissime crescit, intelligitur Baptismus seu fides.
paras.en: [[44:9|Myrrh and stacte and cassia perfume thy garments, from the ivory houses|Myrrha et gutta et casia a vestimentis tuis, a domibus eburneis]]. By myrrh, which is bitter, preserves dead bodies from corruption and keeps off worms, the mortification of the flesh is understood, which drives out the stench of concupiscence and the filth of vice, as the Apostle says: [[Rom 8:1|There is now therefore no condemnation to them that are in Christ Jesus, who walk not according to the flesh|Nihil damnationis est his qui sunt in Christo Jesu, qui non secundum carnem ambulant]]. And again: [[Rom 8:13|if you live according to the flesh, you shall die: but if by the Spirit you mortify the deeds of the flesh, you shall live|Si secundum carnem vixeritis, moriemini; si autem spiritu facta carnis mortificaveritis, vivetis]]. By stacte [*gutta*, literally "a drop", an aromatic gum], which is fragrant and takes away swellings and hardness, humility is signified. Hence Solomon says: [[Prov 28:14|he that is hardened in mind shall fall into evil|Qui mentis est duræ, corruet in mala]]; but [[Prov 29:23|glory shall uphold the humble of spirit|humilem spiritu suscipiet gloria]]. By cassia, which grows in moist places and rises very high, Baptism, or faith, is understood.

paras.t: Est igitur sensus: Myrrha et gutta et casia, id est virtutes per has species aromaticas significatæ, a vestimentis tuis, id est a natura tua humana, o Christe, quæ fuit quasi vestimentum divinæ tuæ naturæ, procedunt et dantur Ecclesiæ tuæ: omnis enim sufficientia ejus ex te est. Et hæ virtutes, quantum ad actum suum, sunt non solum a vestimentis tuis, sed etiam a domibus eburneis, id est a castis atque constantibus fidelium mentibus. Oportet enim nos cooperari gratiæ Dei, et ideo actus virtutum sunt simul a te, et ab hominibus virtuosis: quibus ait Apostolus, Hortamur vos ne in vacuum gratiam Dei recipiatis. Et ad Timotheum: Noli negligere gratiam quæ in te est, quæ data est tibi.
paras.en: The sense, then, is: [[44:9|Myrrh and stacte and cassia|Myrrha et gutta et casia]], that is, the virtues signified by these aromatic spices, [[44:9|perfume thy garments|a vestimentis tuis]] [the Latin is *a vestimentis tuis*, "from thy garments"]: that is, from thy human nature, O Christ, which was as it were the garment of thy divine nature, they proceed and are given to thy Church; for all her sufficiency is from thee. And these virtues, as regards their acts, are not only from thy garments but also [[44:9|from the ivory houses|a domibus eburneis]], that is, from the chaste and steadfast minds of the faithful. For we must cooperate with the grace of God, and therefore the acts of the virtues are at once from thee and from virtuous men, to whom the Apostle says: We [[2 Cor 6:1|do exhort you that you receive not the grace of God in vain|Hortamur vos ne in vacuum gratiam Dei recipiatis]]. And to Timothy: [[1 Tim 4:14|Neglect not the grace that is in thee, which was given thee|Noli negligere gratiam quæ in te est, quæ data est tibi]].

paras.t: Ex quibus virtutibus delectaverunt te, id est, tibi complacuerunt, filiæ regum, id est animæ religiosæ, mundo et carni atque dæmonibus dominantes, in honore tuo, id est, ad honorem nominis tui opera bona agentes. Solæ enim virtutes faciunt intellectualem creaturam Deo acceptam et gratam. Ad litteram quoque multæ filiæ regum, videlicet Catharina, Barbara, atque sacratissima Ursula cum suis felicissimis ac præamandis sodalibus, Christo propter prædictas virtutes delectabiliter placuerunt, ita ut ejus deliciæ sint esse cum talibus regum filiabus.
paras.en: [[44:9|out of which|Ex quibus]] virtues [[44:10|The daughters of kings|filiæ regum]], that is, religious souls, masters of the world, the flesh and the demons, [[44:10|have delighted thee|delectaverunt te]], that is, have been pleasing to thee, [[44:10|in thy glory|in honore tuo]] [literally "in thy honour"], that is, doing good works to the honour of thy name. For the virtues alone make an intellectual creature acceptable and pleasing to God. According to the letter also, many daughters of kings, namely Catherine, Barbara, and the most holy Ursula with her most happy and most lovable companions, delightfully pleased Christ by reason of the virtues named, so that his delights are to be with such daughters of kings[[Prov 8:31||]].

paras.t: Adstitit, o Christe, regina, id est sponsa tua sancta Ecclesia, a dextris tuis, id est in potioribus gratiæ tuæ muneribus, et in prospero beneplacito tuo, in vestitu deaurato, id est, in caritate divina sanctis operibus adornata, circumdata varietate, id est, undique perornata diversis charismatibus gratiæ Spiritus Sancti, atque diversis generibus populorum, statuum, officiorum ac graduum.
paras.en: There [[44:10|stood|Adstitit]], O Christ, [[44:10|the queen|regina]], that is, thy spouse, holy Church, [[44:10|on thy right hand|a dextris tuis]], that is, in the greater gifts of thy grace and in thy favourable good pleasure, [[44:10|in gilded clothing|in vestitu deaurato]], that is, in divine charity adorned with holy works, [[44:10|surrounded with variety|circumdata varietate]], that is, adorned on every side with the diverse charisms of the grace of the Holy Ghost, and with diverse kinds of peoples, states, offices and ranks.

paras.t: Adstat quippe Christo sancta Ecclesia tanquam parata obedire ejus imperio, et cooperans gratiæ sui Sponsi, filios suos docendo, corrigendo, perficiendo. Stat quoque a dextris ejus, et non a sinistris, tanquam Sponso suo carissima, quemadmodum dicit et Apostolus: Christus dilexit Ecclesiam, et tradidit semetipsum pro ea, ut illam sanctificaret, mundans illam lavacro aquæ in verbo, ut exhiberet sibi gloriosam Ecclesiam, non habentem maculam neque rugam. De hac Christi sponsa, matre Ecclesia et regina, in Apocalypsi scriptum est: Signum magnum apparuit in cœlo: mulier amicta sole, et luna sub pedibus ejus, et in capite ejus corona stellarum duodecim; et clamavit parturiens ut pareret. Hæc enim mulier amicta est sole, id est Christo, sicut ait Apostolus, Induimini Dominum Jesum Christum; et luna, id est defectus et inconstantia, sub pedibus ejus. Aitque in Apocalypsi Joannes: Venerunt nuptiæ Agni, et uxor ejus præparavit se. Hæc autem regina induta est vestitu deaurato. Nam per aurum intelligitur caritas, juxta illud: Suadeo tibi emere aurum ignitum, probatum. Hoc enim tepido dicitur.
paras.en: For holy Church stands by Christ as one ready to obey his command, and cooperating with the grace of her Spouse by teaching, correcting and perfecting her children. And she stands on his right hand and not on his left, as most dear to her Spouse, as the Apostle too says: [[Eph 5:25|Christ also loved the church and delivered himself up for it|Christus dilexit Ecclesiam, et tradidit semetipsum pro ea]], [[Eph 5:26|That he might sanctify it, cleansing it by the laver of water in the word|ut illam sanctificaret, mundans illam lavacro aquæ in verbo]], [[Eph 5:27|That he might present it to himself, a glorious church, not having spot or wrinkle|ut exhiberet sibi gloriosam Ecclesiam, non habentem maculam neque rugam]]. Of this spouse of Christ, our mother the Church and queen, it is written in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 12:1|a great sign appeared in heaven: A woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars|Signum magnum apparuit in cœlo: mulier amicta sole, et luna sub pedibus ejus, et in capite ejus corona stellarum duodecim]]; and [[Apoc 12:2|she cried travailing in birth: and was in pain to be delivered|clamavit parturiens ut pareret]]. For this woman is clothed with the sun, that is, with Christ, as the Apostle says: [[Rom 13:14|put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ|Induimini Dominum Jesum Christum]]; and the moon, that is, failing and inconstancy, is under her feet. And John says in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 19:7|the marriage of the Lamb is come: and his wife hath prepared herself|Venerunt nuptiæ Agni, et uxor ejus præparavit se]]. And this queen is clad in gilded clothing. For by gold charity is understood, according to that saying: [[Apoc 3:18|I counsel thee to buy of me gold, fire tried|Suadeo tibi emere aurum ignitum, probatum]]. For this is said to the lukewarm one.

paras.t: Deinde huic reginæ Christique sponsæ dicitur: Audi verbum Dei: Beati enim qui audiunt verbum Dei, et custodiunt illud; o filia in Christo, ex aqua et Spiritu Sancto regenerata; et vide, id est, per fidem considera omnia quæ Christo sponso tuo sunt placita, et inclina aurem tuam, ut ei obedias; et obliviscere populum tuum, id est, inordinatum affectum hominum tibi notorum depone, et domum patris tui, id est, societatem pravorum fuge, et propinquos carnaliter diligere cessa, quatenus Deo tota adhæreas.
paras.en: Then it is said to this queen and spouse of Christ: [[44:11|Hearken|Audi]] to the word of God (for [[Luke 11:28|blessed are they who hear the word of God and keep it|Beati enim qui audiunt verbum Dei, et custodiunt illud]]), [[44:11|O daughter|filia]] in Christ, reborn of water and the Holy Ghost; [[44:11|and see|et vide]], that is, consider by faith all that is pleasing to Christ thy Spouse, [[44:11|and incline thy ear|et inclina aurem tuam]], so as to obey him; [[44:11|and forget thy people|et obliviscere populum tuum]], that is, lay aside an inordinate affection for the people known to thee, [[44:11|and thy father's house|et domum patris tui]], that is, flee the company of the wicked and cease to love thy kinsfolk carnally, so that thou mayest cleave wholly to God.

paras.t: Quod si feceris, tunc Et concupiscet rex decorem tuum, id est, Christus pulchritudinem mentis tuæ amabit, quoniam ipse est Dominus Deus tuus, cui soli debes velle placere, nec alium sponsum ei præferre; et adorabunt eum omnes in ipsum credentes: quemadmodum in Daniele scriptum est, Omnes populi, tribus, et linguæ servient ei. Ecce hic rursus testatur Psalmographus, regem de quo nunc loquitur, scilicet Christum, esse Deum, imo et verum Deum, in eo quod ait, Et adorabunt eum. Adoratio namque proprie sumpta, convenit soli vero Deo. Propter hanc autem amorosam concupiscentiam, qua Christus amat decorem Sponsæ suæ, in Canticis ipse ait: Vulnerasti cor meum, soror mea, sponsa, vulnerasti cor meum; et, Aperi mihi, soror mea, amica mea, columba mea; et, Pone me ut signaculum super cor tuum, ut signaculum super brachia tua, quia fortis est ut mors dilectio.
paras.en: If thou dost this, then [[44:12|And the king shall greatly desire thy beauty|Et concupiscet rex decorem tuum]], that is, Christ will love the beauty of thy soul, [[44:12|for he is the Lord thy God|quoniam ipse est Dominus Deus tuus]], whom alone thou oughtest to wish to please, preferring no other spouse to him; [[44:12|and him they shall adore|et adorabunt eum]], all who believe in him, as it is written in Daniel: [[Dan 7:14|all peoples, tribes, and tongues shall serve him|Omnes populi, tribus, et linguæ servient ei]]. See how here again the Psalmist testifies that the king of whom he now speaks, namely Christ, is God, and indeed true God, when he says: [[44:12|and him they shall adore|Et adorabunt eum]]. For adoration, taken properly, belongs to the true God alone. Because of this loving desire [*concupiscentia*, from the verse's *concupiscet*, "shall greatly desire"], with which Christ loves the beauty of his Spouse, he says himself in the Canticle: [[Cant 4:9|Thou hast wounded my heart, my sister, my spouse, thou hast wounded my heart|Vulnerasti cor meum, soror mea, sponsa, vulnerasti cor meum]]; and: [[Cant 5:2|Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove|Aperi mihi, soror mea, amica mea, columba mea]]; and: [[Cant 8:6|Put me as a seal upon thy heart, as a seal upon thy arm, for love is strong as death|Pone me ut signaculum super cor tuum, ut signaculum super brachia tua, quia fortis est ut mors dilectio]].

paras.t: Et filiæ Tyri in muneribus. Tyrus civitas erat famosa ac nobilis, vicina Judææ atque pagana: idcirco per Tyrum designantur gentiles. Et est sensus: Non solum ex Judæis conversi Christum adorabunt, sed et filiæ Tyri in muneribus, id est gentiles ad fidem conversi, Christum adorabunt, munera offerendo, id est se ipsos et sacrificium novæ legis, ac alias oblationes tempore novæ legis consuetas ac licitas. Et hoc est quod Isaias ait: Cognoscetur Dominus ab Ægypto, et cognoscent Ægyptii Dominum, et colent eum in hostiis et muneribus. Per hæc enim atque similia insinuatur tota gentilitas convertenda ad Christum, secundum quod legitur: In die illa radix Jesse qui stat in signum populorum, ipsum gentes deprecabuntur, et erit sepulcrum ejus gloriosum. Hæc in Jesu Nazareno verissime sunt impleta. Nam et Tyrus illa multo tempore christiano cultui dedita fuit.
paras.en: [[44:13|And the daughters of Tyre with gifts|Et filiæ Tyri in muneribus]]. Tyre was a famous and noble city, near Judea and pagan; therefore by Tyre the Gentiles are signified. And the sense is: not only those converted from the Jews will adore Christ, but also [[44:13|the daughters of Tyre with gifts|filiæ Tyri in muneribus]], that is, the Gentiles converted to the faith, will adore Christ by offering gifts, that is, themselves and the sacrifice of the new law, and the other offerings customary and lawful in the time of the new law. And this is what Isaias says: [[Is 19:21|the Lord shall be known by Egypt, and the Egyptians shall know the Lord|Cognoscetur Dominus ab Ægypto, et cognoscent Ægyptii Dominum]], [[Is 19:21|and shall worship him with sacrifices and offerings|et colent eum in hostiis et muneribus]]. For by these and similar words it is intimated that all the Gentile world is to be converted to Christ, according to what we read: [[Is 11:10|In that day the root of Jesse, who standeth for an ensign of the people, him the Gentiles shall beseech, and his sepulchre shall be glorious|In die illa radix Jesse qui stat in signum populorum, ipsum gentes deprecabuntur, et erit sepulcrum ejus gloriosum]]. These things were most truly fulfilled in Jesus of Nazareth. For that Tyre too was given to Christian worship for a long time.

paras.t: Vultum tuum deprecabuntur omnes divites plebis: id est, te ipsam seu tuam participationem atque præsentiam, o Ecclesia Christi, orabunt omnes gentes ad fidem conversæ: quæ spiritualiter divites sunt in caritate et gratia. Jam enim videmus, quod magni et parvi omnesque fideles, deprecantur pastores ac sacerdotes Ecclesiæ, quatenus orent pro se, et verbum Dei sacramentaque Christi sibi communicent, sicut apud Malachiam habetur: Labia sacerdotis custodiunt scientiam, et legem ex ore ejus requirent. Vel sic: Vultum tuum, o Ecclesia, deprecabuntur omnes divites plebis, ita ut vultus tuus erit id quod petent, non id a quo petent. Ut sit sensus: Deprecabuntur a Deo vultum tuum, quatenus pertineant ad gregem credentium, quoniam extra Ecclesiam non est alicui salus, sicut nec extra arcam Noe quisquam a diluvio salvatus est.
paras.en: [[44:13|all the rich among the people, shall entreat thy countenance|Vultum tuum deprecabuntur omnes divites plebis]]: that is, all the nations converted to the faith, who are spiritually rich in charity and grace, will pray to thee thyself, O Church of Christ, or for a share in thee and thy presence. For we see already that great and small and all the faithful entreat the pastors and priests of the Church to pray for them and to impart to them the word of God and the sacraments of Christ, as we have it in Malachias: [[Mal 2:7|the lips of the priests shall keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law at his mouth|Labia sacerdotis custodiunt scientiam, et legem ex ore ejus requirent]]. Or thus: [[44:13|thy countenance|Vultum tuum]], O Church, [[44:13|all the rich among the people, shall entreat|deprecabuntur omnes divites plebis]], so that thy countenance will be what they ask for, not the one of whom they ask it.
